2.1 — Hydrostatic Forces on Plane Surfaces

Resultant force on submerged surfaces • Center of pressure • Worked examples: gates, hinges & stops

Why Hydrostatic Forces?

In Chapter 1 we learned that pressure increases linearly with depth in a static incompressible fluid. That pressure acts on every submerged surface — dam faces, lock gates, tank walls, submarine hulls. To design these structures, we need to answer two questions:

(1) What is the total hydrostatic force (the "resultant force") on the surface?
(2) Where does that resultant force act (the "center of pressure")?

Knowing both the magnitude and the location of the resultant force lets us perform static equilibrium analysis on structures — finding hinge reactions, bolt forces, required counterweights, and so on.

Force on a Horizontal Surface

For a flat, horizontal surface at depth \(H\) below the free surface, the pressure is uniform across the entire area because every point is at the same depth. The resultant force is simply pressure times area:

Resultant Force — Horizontal Surface
\[ F_b = p_b \, A_b = \gamma H \, A_b \]
\(F_b\) — resultant hydrostatic force on the bottom surface [N] \(p_b = \gamma H\) — uniform gage pressure at depth \(H\) [Pa] \(A_b\) — area of the horizontal surface [m²] \(\gamma = \rho g\) — specific weight of the fluid [N/m³]

Because the pressure is uniform, the resultant passes through the centroid of the surface — the center of pressure coincides with the centroid. But what about inclined or vertical surfaces where pressure varies with depth?

Force on an Inclined Plane Surface

When a plane surface is tilted at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, the pressure on it varies linearly from top to bottom (since depth increases along the surface). The hydrostatic pressure acts perpendicular to the surface at every point, and its magnitude increases with depth.

Figure 2.1.1 — Inclined plane surface at angle \(\theta\). Side view shows the free surface, depth \(h(x,y)\), centroid depth \(h_{\text{CG}}\), and the resultant force \(F = p_{\text{CG}} A\). Plan view shows the centroid (CG) and center of pressure (CP) on the surface.

We define a coordinate \(\xi\) measured along the inclined surface from the free-surface intersection line. The depth at any point relates to \(\xi\) by \(h = \xi \sin\theta\). A local coordinate system \((x, y)\) is centered at the centroid (CG) of the surface, with \(y\) pointing up-slope (toward the free surface).

Resultant Force

Derivation of Resultant Force

The total force on the inclined surface is the integral of pressure over area:

\[ F = \int p \, dA = \int (p_a + \gamma h) \, dA = p_a A + \gamma \int h \, dA \]

Substituting \(h = \xi \sin\theta\):

\[ F = p_a A + \gamma \sin\theta \int \xi \, dA \]

The integral \(\int \xi \, dA\) is recognized as \(\xi_{\text{CG}} \cdot A\) by the definition of the centroid:

\[ \xi_{\text{CG}} = \frac{1}{A} \int \xi \, dA \]

Since \(h_{\text{CG}} = \xi_{\text{CG}} \sin\theta\), we arrive at:

\[ F = p_a A + \gamma \sin\theta \, \xi_{\text{CG}} \, A = (p_a + \gamma h_{\text{CG}}) A = p_{\text{CG}} \, A \]
Resultant Force on Inclined Plane Surface
\[ \boxed{F = p_{\text{CG}} \, A = (p_a + \gamma h_{\text{CG}}) \, A} \]
\(F\) — resultant hydrostatic force [N] \(p_{\text{CG}}\) — pressure at the centroid of the surface [Pa] \(p_a\) — surface pressure (atmospheric, or tank pressure) [Pa] \(\gamma = \rho g\) — specific weight [N/m³] \(h_{\text{CG}}\) — vertical depth of the centroid below the free surface [m] \(A\) — area of the submerged surface [m²]
★ Key Insight

The resultant force equals the pressure at the centroid times the area — as if the entire surface were at the centroid depth. This is exact for linear pressure distributions (which is what we have in hydrostatics). The centroid is the "average location" of the area, and the force formula effectively averages the linearly-varying pressure over the surface.

Center of Pressure

The resultant force \(F\) does not act at the centroid — it acts at the center of pressure (CP), which is always below the centroid (toward the high-pressure side). This is because the deeper portions of the surface carry more pressure, pulling the effective point of action downward.

To find the CP, we balance the moment of the resultant force about the centroid with the integral of elemental moments \(y \cdot p \, dA\).

Figure 2.1.2 — The pressure distribution on an arbitrary inclined surface. The average pressure acts at the centroid (CG), but the resultant force acts at the center of pressure (CP), which is displaced toward the high-pressure (deeper) side.
Derivation of Center of Pressure

Taking moments about the centroid (where \(y\) is measured from the centroid toward the free surface):

\[ F \, y_{\text{CP}} = \int y \, p \, dA = \int y\,(p_a + \gamma \xi \sin\theta)\,dA \]

The \(p_a\) term vanishes because \(\int y \, dA = 0\) (definition of centroid). Substituting \(\xi = \xi_{\text{CG}} - y\):

\[ F \, y_{\text{CP}} = \gamma \sin\theta \left(\xi_{\text{CG}} \underbrace{\int y \, dA}_{= \, 0} - \int y^2 \, dA\right) = -\gamma \sin\theta \, I_{xx} \]

where \(I_{xx} = \int y^2 \, dA\) is the second moment of area about the centroidal \(x\)-axis. Dividing by \(F = p_{\text{CG}} A\):

\[ y_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{\gamma \sin\theta \, I_{xx}}{p_{\text{CG}} \, A} \]

Similarly, for the horizontal offset \(x_{\text{CP}}\) (involving the product of inertia \(I_{xy}\)):

\[ x_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{\gamma \sin\theta \, I_{xy}}{p_{\text{CG}} \, A} \]
Center of Pressure Location
\[ \boxed{y_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{\gamma \sin\theta \; I_{xx}}{p_{\text{CG}}\, A}} \qquad \boxed{x_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{\gamma \sin\theta \; I_{xy}}{p_{\text{CG}}\, A}} \]
\(y_{\text{CP}}\) — distance from centroid to CP along the surface (negative = below CG) [m] \(x_{\text{CP}}\) — horizontal offset of CP from CG [m] \(I_{xx}\) — 2nd moment of area about centroidal \(x\)-axis [m⁴] \(I_{xy}\) — product of inertia about centroidal axes [m⁴] \(\theta\) — angle of the surface from horizontal [rad or deg] \(p_{\text{CG}}\) — pressure at the centroid [Pa]
★ Key Insight — CP Is Always Below CG

The negative sign in \(y_{\text{CP}}\) means the center of pressure is always displaced toward the high-pressure (deeper) side of the surface relative to the centroid. The deeper the surface (larger \(h_{\text{CG}}\)), the closer CP approaches CG — at great depth the pressure distribution becomes nearly uniform and the two points converge.

Gage Pressure Simplification

When the surface of the fluid is open to the atmosphere, we can set \(p_a = 0\) (gage) and \(p_{\text{CG}} = \gamma h_{\text{CG}}\). The formulas simplify to:

Resultant Force & CP — Open Surface (Gage Pressure)
\[ F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A \qquad y_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{I_{xx} \sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A} \qquad x_{\text{CP}} = -\frac{I_{xy} \sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A} \]
These are the most-used forms for problems with a free surface open to the atmosphere.

Area Moments of Inertia — Common Shapes

The center of pressure equations require \(I_{xx}\) and \(I_{xy}\) about the centroidal axes. Here are the two shapes you will use most often:

Rectangle (b × L)
\[ A = bL \qquad I_{xx} = \frac{bL^3}{12} \qquad I_{xy} = 0 \]

\(b\) = width, \(L\) = length (along slope direction). CG at geometric center. \(I_{xy} = 0\) by symmetry.

Circle (radius R)
\[ A = \pi R^2 \qquad I_{xx} = \frac{\pi R^4}{4} \qquad I_{xy} = 0 \]

CG at center. \(I_{xy} = 0\) by symmetry. For any shape with an axis of symmetry aligned with the slope, \(I_{xy} = 0\) and \(x_{\text{CP}} = 0\).

★ Exam Warning

For symmetric shapes (rectangle, circle, ellipse) aligned with the slope direction, \(I_{xy} = 0\) so \(x_{\text{CP}} = 0\) — the center of pressure lies on the line of symmetry. You only need to find \(y_{\text{CP}}\). Non-symmetric shapes (triangles, trapezoids) or surfaces rotated relative to the slope direction will have \(I_{xy} \neq 0\).

Worked Examples

Example 2.1 — Seawater Gate (Inclined)

Problem: A gate is 5 ft wide, hinged at point B, and rests against a smooth wall at point A. The seawater has specific weight \(\gamma = 64\) lbf/ft³. The gate spans 8 ft horizontally and 6 ft vertically, with the top edge (A) at 15 ft depth. Find: (a) the resultant force, (b) the wall reaction P at A, (c) the hinge reactions at B.

Figure 2.1.3 — Gate AB hinged at B, resting against a smooth wall at A. Seawater depth to A is 15 ft. Gate dimensions: 8 ft horizontal, 6 ft vertical.
Show Solution

Formulas needed: \(F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A\), \(\; l = -y_{\text{CP}} = \dfrac{I_{xx}\sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A}\), moment equilibrium \(\sum M = 0\), force balance \(\sum F = 0\).

(a) Gate geometry and resultant force:

Gate length: \(L = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10\) ft. Gate area: \(A = 5 \times 10 = 50\) ft². The angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\sin\theta = 6/10 = 0.6\), \(\cos\theta = 8/10 = 0.8\).

The centroid is at the midpoint of the gate. Depth of CG below the free surface:

\[ h_{\text{CG}} = 15 - \tfrac{6}{2} \cdot 1 = 15 - 3 = 12 \text{ ft} \]

(The CG is 3 ft above B vertically, so 15 − 3 = 12 ft below the surface.)

Resultant force:

\[ F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A = (64)(12)(50) = \boxed{38{,}400 \text{ lbf}} \]

(b) Center of pressure and wall reaction P:

For the rectangular gate: \(I_{xx} = \dfrac{bL^3}{12} = \dfrac{(5)(10)^3}{12} = 417 \text{ ft}^4\), \(\;I_{xy} = 0\).

Distance from CG to CP:

\[ l = -y_{\text{CP}} = \frac{I_{xx}\sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A} = \frac{(417)(0.6)}{(12)(50)} = 0.417 \text{ ft} \]

The resultant \(F\) acts 0.417 ft below the CG along the gate, which is \(5 - 0.417 = 4.583\) ft from B along the gate.

Figure 2.1.4 — Free body diagram of gate AB showing resultant force F, wall reaction P, hinge reactions \(B_x\) and \(B_z\), centroid (CG), and center of pressure (CP).

Taking moments about B (\(\sum M_B = 0\)):

\[ P \cdot L\sin\theta - F(5 - l) = 0 \] \[ P(6) - 38{,}400(4.583) = 0 \] \[ \boxed{P = 29{,}300 \text{ lbf}} \]

(c) Hinge reactions at B:

Horizontal equilibrium: \(\sum F_x = B_x + F\sin\theta - P = 0\)

\[ B_x = P - F\sin\theta = 29{,}300 - 38{,}400(0.6) = \boxed{6{,}300 \text{ lbf}} \]

Vertical equilibrium: \(\sum F_z = B_z - F\cos\theta = 0\)

\[ B_z = F\cos\theta = 38{,}400(0.8) = \boxed{30{,}700 \text{ lbf}} \]
Example 2.2 — Vertical Gate with Hinge and Stop

Problem: Gate AB is 5 ft wide (into the screen), hinged at A, and restrained by a stop at B. The water depth is \(h = 9.5\) ft, water at 20°C (\(\gamma = 62.4\) lbf/ft³). The gate is 4 ft tall, vertical (\(\theta = 90°\)). Find: (a) the resultant hydrostatic force, (b) the force on stop B, (c) the reactions at A.

Show Solution

Formulas needed: \(F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A\), \(\; l = -y_{\text{CP}} = \dfrac{I_{xx}\sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A}\), \(\sum M_A = 0\), \(\sum F_x = 0\).

(a) Resultant force:

Gate dimensions: 5 ft × 4 ft, \(A = 20\) ft². The top of the gate (hinge A) is at depth \(h - 4 = 5.5\) ft. The centroid is 2 ft below A:

\[ h_{\text{CG}} = 9.5 - 4 + 2 = 7.5 \text{ ft} \] \[ F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A = (62.4)(7.5)(20) = \boxed{9{,}360 \text{ lbf}} \]

(Note: the slides use \(\gamma = 64.4\) lbf/ft³ for water at 20°C — small differences in \(\gamma\) come from rounding. Use whichever value is given.)

(b) Center of pressure and stop reaction:

For the 5 ft × 4 ft rectangle: \(I_{xx} = \dfrac{(5)(4)^3}{12} = 26.67\) ft⁴. With \(\theta = 90°\) (\(\sin 90° = 1\)):

\[ l = -y_{\text{CP}} = \frac{I_{xx}\sin\theta}{h_{\text{CG}} A} = \frac{(26.67)(1)}{(7.5)(20)} = 0.178 \text{ ft} \]

The CP is 0.178 ft below the CG. Distance from A to the force: \(4/2 + 0.178 = 2.178\) ft.

Moment about A (\(\sum M_A = 0\)):

\[ B_x(4) - F(2.178) = 0 \implies B_x = \frac{9{,}360 \times 2.178}{4} = \boxed{5{,}100 \text{ lbf}} \]

(c) Reactions at A:

Horizontal equilibrium: \(\sum F_x = -B_x + F - A_x = 0\)

\[ A_x = F - B_x = 9{,}360 - 5{,}100 = \boxed{4{,}260 \text{ lbf}} \]

The vertical reaction \(A_y\) depends on the weight of the gate (not given here).

★ Problem-Solving Strategy — Hydrostatic Gate Problems

Step 1: Find the gate geometry — length \(L\), width \(b\), angle \(\theta\), area \(A\).
Step 2: Find the centroid depth \(h_{\text{CG}}\) below the free surface.
Step 3: Compute the resultant: \(F = \gamma h_{\text{CG}} A\).
Step 4: Compute \(I_{xx}\) (and \(I_{xy}\) if asymmetric), then find the CG-to-CP distance \(l\).
Step 5: Draw a FBD of the gate. Apply moment equilibrium about the hinge to find the reaction at the other support. Then use force balance for the hinge reactions.
